newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan views may hurt U.S. junk bond fund flows.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan views may hurt U.S. junk bond fund flows.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's warning on Wednesday that junk bonds may be overvalued might hurt the market over the long term by weakening cash flows into high-yield mutual funds, said market experts.
"You could see some price deterioration next week if mutual fund inflows slow dramatically," said Paul Greenberg, head of high-yield research at Bear Stearns & Co Inc.
He added, "It won't have an effect in the short term as money managers have nowhere else to put their money."
"In the short-term Greenspan's comments should not cause a material change," said Mark Durbiano, head of high-yield bond investing at Federated Investors.

He said, "The only way Greenspan can impact the market on a longer-term basis is to preemtively raise rates in order to dramtically slow the economy. Only a recession would cause the fundamental underpinnings of the market to deteriorate."
Traders said Greenspan's comments were having no effect on prices of U.S. high yield bonds as of 1100EST/1600GMT.
A trader said, "I don't think there is tremendous down-side risk today."
The Treasury market's reaction to Greenspan's speech was far more negative with the price of the 30-year long-bond dropping 1-1/4 points.

Stock market prices were also hurt, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling over 100 points soon after the Fed Chairman's testimony, then bouncing back slightly to about 6975, shortly before noon, down about 62 points from Tuesday's close.

In testimony given to members of the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday morning, Greenspan delivered an upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy but voiced concerns about soaring prices in the financial markets.
In his testimony, Greenspan said, "Caution also seems warranted by the narrow yield spreads that suggest perceptions of low risk, possibly unrealistically low risk."
He said optimism about business activity "has become especially evident in quality spreads on high-yield corporate bonds -- what we used to call 'junk bonds.'"

Analysts noted that spreads on high-yield bonds have reached historically tight levels in recent weeks, propelled by positive views on the economy as well as tremendous cash inflows into high-yield mutual funds.
Sam DeRosa-Farag, director of high-yield strategy at Chase Securities, said it unclear how Greenspan's comments would affect mutual fund flows into the high-yield market.
"I don't think in general what Greenspan is alluding to here is anything people are not aware of. Spreads have been tightening across the board in all capital markets."

Edward Mally, head of high-yield research at CIBC Wood Gundy said, "While we look at mutual fund flows as a barometer, it is not the sole driving force in the high-yield market. There continues to be flows of more stable money from pension funds".
Bear Stearns' Greenberg noted the high-yield market has recently benefitted from an improved image which has drawn a more diverse range of insitutional investors.
"A lot of the (recent) spread tightening is due to the fact that junk bonds are being seen as a more legitimate area of putting money. High-grade investors are increasingly looking to our market."
He added, "A lot of these investors will look at any weakness as a buying opportunity."
-Douglas Brown, 212-859-1662
